name: Le Chatelier's Principle
what: This subtopic covers Le Chatelier's principle and its application to predict how changes in temperature, concentration, pressure, volume, and dilution affect the position of equilibrium. It also addresses the effect of catalysts and the role of K in predicting shifts.
why: Le Chatelier's principle is central to VCE Chemistry Unit 3 and is applied across a wide range of question types. It connects qualitative reasoning about equilibrium shifts with quantitative predictions about K values and product yields.

items.title: I can state Le Chatelier's principle
items.what: Le Chatelier's principle states that if an equilibrium system is subjected to a change, the system will adjust itself to partially oppose that change and restore equilibrium.
items.why: A precise, memorised statement of this principle is frequently required as the first step in extended response questions. The word 'partially' is important - the system does not fully undo the change.
items.example: If extra nitrogen gas is added to the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) = 2NH3(g), the system partially opposes this by consuming some of the added nitrogen through the forward reaction, producing more ammonia until a new equilibrium is established.

items.title: I can predict the effect of a temperature change on the position of equilibrium
items.what: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction of a reaction. Decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction. A useful strategy is to write 'heat' as a reactant (endothermic) or product (exothermic) and treat it like any other species being added or removed.
items.why: Temperature changes are one of the most commonly tested scenarios in VCE. The answer depends on both the direction of temperature change and whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, requiring students to apply careful logic.
items.example: For 2NO2(g) = N2O4(g) with delta H = -57 kJ mol^-1 (exothermic), increasing temperature is like adding heat to the product side. The system opposes this by favouring the reverse reaction, producing more NO2 and decreasing the amount of N2O4.

items.title: I can determine the effect of temperature change on the equilibrium constant K
items.what: Temperature is the only condition that changes the value of K. If a temperature change favours the forward reaction, K increases. If it favours the reverse reaction, K decreases.
items.why: Students frequently state incorrectly that K changes when concentration or pressure is altered. Knowing that only temperature changes K is a key distinction tested directly in VCE examinations.
items.example: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) = 2NH3(g) with delta H = -92 kJ mol^-1, increasing temperature favours the reverse (endothermic) reaction, so the concentration of NH3 decreases relative to reactants. The value of K therefore decreases at higher temperatures.

items.title: I can predict the effect of a change in volume on the position of equilibrium
items.what: Decreasing volume increases pressure, which the system opposes by favouring the reaction that produces fewer moles of gas. Increasing volume decreases pressure, and the system favours the side with more moles of gas.
items.why: Volume and pressure changes are tested in both multiple-choice and extended response questions. The effect depends on comparing the total moles of gas on each side of the equation, so students must count gas particles carefully.
items.example: For N2(g) + 2O2(g) = 2NO2(g), the reactant side has 3 moles of gas and the product side has 2. If the volume is halved (pressure increases), the system favours the forward reaction to reduce the number of gas molecules and lower the pressure.

items.title: I can predict the effect of adding or removing a reactant or product on the position of equilibrium
items.what: Adding a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right (forward reaction favoured). Removing a reactant shifts it to the left. Adding a product shifts it to the left (reverse reaction favoured). Removing a product shifts it to the right.
items.why: Concentration changes are the most straightforward application of Le Chatelier's principle, but students must be systematic. This skill is also the basis for understanding how continuous removal of a product can be used industrially to drive a reaction toward completion.
items.example: In the reaction Fe3+(aq) + SCN-(aq) = FeSCN2+(aq), if Fe(NO3)3 is added, the increased concentration of Fe3+ causes the forward reaction to be favoured. The mixture becomes darker red as more FeSCN2+ is produced.
